extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, historians/philosophers of mathematics, and educated readers interested in foundations and practice of mathematics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts the standards, criteria and evaluative principles Von Neumann discusses for what counts as rigour, success, and healthy practice in mathematics (including foundations, aesthetics, empirical ties, and problem selection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuitionistic revision of mathematical rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: A system of mathematics (intuitionism) which avoids the philosophically objectionable uses of 'general validity' and 'existence' and thereby eliminates the contradictions arising in set theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Brouwer's intuitionism removed set-theoretic contradictions but at the cost of invalidating or complicating about fifty percent of modern mathematics (notably parts of analysis). Adopting such exigent standards typically reduces generality and elegance of deduction; many mathematicians acknowledged the critique but continued to work classically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hilbert's metamathematical justification program
rubrics_metrics.description: The idea that classical (pre-intuitionistic) mathematics could be justified by showing, within a rigorously formulated metatheory, that classical procedures cannot lead to contradictions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hilbert proposed describing classical mathematics within a more restrictive system and proving that classical methods never produce contradictions. The program envisaged a demonstration of the consistency of classical mathematics based on intuitionistically acceptable arguments, but success was uncertain and technically difficult.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gödel's incompleteness/limit on internal consistency proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Gödel's essential result: if a system of mathematics is consistent, that consistency cannot be demonstrated using only the procedures of that same system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This theorem meets the strictest criteria of mathematical rigour (including the intuitionistic one) and substantially undermined the feasibility of Hilbert's program; Von Neumann (and many others) regarded this as showing Hilbert's program to be essentially hopeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pragmatic acceptance of classical mathematics
rubrics_metrics.description: Even without an absolute, a priori guarantee of reliability, classical mathematics was adopted because it produced results that were both elegant and useful and seemed to rest on as sound a foundation as certain empirical sciences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most mathematicians continued to use classical methods despite foundational doubts; pragmatic and empirical analogies (e.g., the existence of the electron) were invoked to justify continued reliance on classical mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience-informed notion of rigour
rubrics_metrics.description: The claim that much of the best mathematical inspiration comes from experience, and that there is no immutable concept of mathematical rigour wholly dissociated from human experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann argues from historical episodes (e.g., set-theoretic difficulties) that mathematical rigour is influenced by practitioners' experiences and cannot be taken as an immutable a priori notion; this cautions against assuming rigid, absolute standards divorced from practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aesthetic criteria of mathematical success
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematical criteria of success are mainly aesthetical: elegance, simplicity, unifying power, architectural/structural beauty, and explanatory simplicity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expected features include: simple and elegant classification of disparate cases; architectural structure (ease of statement versus difficulty of solution); surprising twists that simplify approaches; and, for long deductions, a simple general principle that explains complications. These are akin to criteria in creative arts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unifying and predictive power (borrowed from theoretical physics)
rubrics_metrics.description: A successful theoretical scheme (especially in theoretical physics) should cover many phenomena simply and elegantly and ideally predict phenomena not known when the scheme was developed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann notes these are largely aesthetic criteria but grounded in empirical success in physics; they serve as an analogue for mathematical unification and are a desideratum for theory-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Freedom in problem selection and lack of external obligation
rubrics_metrics.description: Mathematicians enjoy wide freedom in choosing problems; unlike theoretical physicists, mathematical problems are less often objectively given by external phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This freedom means mathematicians' selection criteria are primarily aesthetic or taste-based; mathematics is subdivided into many fields, and an individual mathematician need not (and often cannot) cover more than a fraction of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signs of degeneration (baroque development) and danger of inbreeding
rubrics_metrics.description: As a field moves far from empirical origins, it risks becoming purely aestheticizing, splitting into insignificant branches and becoming a disorganized mass of details ('baroque' or 'very high baroque').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann treats emergence of a baroque style as a danger signal indicating loss of vitality; he cautions that disciplines far removed from empirical roots require corrective measures to avoid degeneration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy: re-injection of empirical ideas to rejuvenate a field
rubrics_metrics.description: The primary remedy for a subject that has become over-abstract or baroque is a rejuvenating return to empirical sources—re-injecting empirical ideas to restore freshness and vitality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann asserts this is a necessary condition to conserve the subject's vitality; historical examples include differential geometry and group theory becoming useful in physics after initially being pursued abstractly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance of abstraction and empirical connection
rubrics_metrics.description: A healthy mathematical field maintains some empirical connections or is kept in check by practitioners with well-developed taste; total abstract inbreeding risks fragmentation and irrelevance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Von Neumann endorses a balance: abstract development is fine if surrounded by correlated subjects with empirical links or guided by taste; otherwise empirical reinsertion is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Management of set-theoretic paradoxes via formal criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain set-theoretic reasonings led to contradictions, but these were 'always easy to spot by certain formal criteria' though philosophically it was unclear why paradoxical parts should be segregated from successful parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical responses (Russell, Weyl, Brouwer) questioned prevailing concepts like 'general validity' and 'existence'; the rubric implies that formal detectability of paradoxes is necessary but philosophically insufficient justification for excluding problematic arguments.
